The company is pitching itself as the agnostic layer where enterprises can work with AI regardless of whether the underlying model comes from companies including Google, Anthropic or OpenAI.
That strategy extends to Cisco’s emerging agentic AI vision, according to Snorre Kjesbu, senior vice president and general manager of Cisco Collaboration.
“Cisco is going to be Switzerland when it comes to working with a lot of players,” he said.
Cisco is already there in the collaboration space, pointing to the company’s interoperability with competing vendors. “We’re thinking the same way also on the agent side, but we need to push innovation as well at the same time,” Kjesbu said.
[Related: 8 New Cisco Workplace And AI Innovations Unveiled At WebexOne 2026]
Cisco is backing that strategy with support for third-party AI models and agents inside its Webex platform, including bring-your-own-LLM capabilities, agent-to-agent interoperability and integrations with external AI providers rather than locking customers into a Cisco-only stack.
Cisco’s integration with Claude, OpenAI-related tools, and other assistants is a shift in strategy for the tech giant, according to Joe Berger, vice president of digital experiences for longtime Cisco top partner World Wide Technology, Maryland Heights, Mo.
“They’re not going to win everything, but they can work with most of the vendors to supply components of it. I think it’s the right approach because I don’t think there’s a winner right now that’s been clearly defined,” he said.
Cisco’s willingness to work across competing platforms is a departure from its longtime approach to the market that’s been evident until recently, Berger said.
“If you look back five years ago, that was a hard pill for them to swallow, being agnostic, and now I think they’re winning more collab deals because they are working with Microsoft and Zoom and now Google. I think that’s the approach they have to take with the broader Cisco portfolio,” he said.
Cisco has realized it has to meet the customers where they are, and the customer might be with a competitor, Berger added.
“If they have that customer-first mindset, ideally, it still brings business to Cisco, whether it’s in a day or in two years. I think it sets them up to be well positioned," he said.
Cisco said it doesn’t want to own the underlying AI model and instead believes its opportunity lies in providing the networking, security, observability and management layers that sit on top of multiple AI platforms. It’s an approach that could be a win for partners, which won’t have to bet their business on one AI model and will be able to build services around multiple models, the company believes.
In fact, Cisco could carve out a unique role for itself as a neutral AI platform because the tech giant isn’t competing with the model vendors, said Lane Irvine, director of strategic alliances for Calgary, Alberta-based Long View Systems, a longtime Cisco partner.
“They want to be the overseer of AI,” Irvine said.
Customers right now are mixing and matching AI models, and because they aren’t standardizing on one, the opportunity exists for an agnostic AI player. It’s similar to the approach that Cisco is taking with its Cloud Control agentic AI platform that became generally available earlier this year, he said.
“They’re going down the path of allowing [Cisco Cloud Control] to control third-party devices. ... They’ll have competitive [vendors] in there and want to be the platform for all of it,” Irvine said.

Networking Stocks Rally as Tech Rebound Lifts AI Gear Makers: Ciena and Arista Climb 4%, but Cisco Barely Moves
AI data center spending is splitting networking stocks into clear winners and laggards, and the gap between Ciena, Arista, and Cisco reveals which part of the network hyperscalers are actually racing to build.
Published October 19, 2026, 2:06pm ET · 3 min read
Market Movers desk. Editor: David Moadel.
Networking hardware is leading a broad technology rebound, and suppliers of optical links and Ethernet switches for AI data centers are drawing the biggest buying. By Monday afternoon, Ciena Corporation (NYSE:CIEN | CIEN Price Prediction) stock was up 4% to $347.48. Meanwhile, Arista Networks (NYSE:ANET) stock also climbed 4%, hitting $183.32 and keeping pace with the gain in Ciena shares.
Shares of Ciena and Arista are running well ahead of the wider technology group. The iShares U.S. Technology ETF (NYSEARCA:IYW) is up 1.29%. Large-cap tech is advancing at a similar pace, with the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) also up 1.31%.
A sharp pullback in Ciena and Arista shares over the prior week came before the bounce. Hyperscaler spending on AI infrastructure remains the core support for Ciena and Arista. Both companies build the networks that move data between and inside AI data centers.
Supply Limits Keep Ciena’s Backlog Growing
Ciena’s fiscal Q3 2026 results showed adjusted EPS of $2.11 against a $1.73 consensus. The company’s revenue rose 37% year over year (YoY) to $1.67 billion.
Cloud providers did the biggest spending for Ciena, accounting for 53% of revenue on 82% YoY growth. Management raised its fiscal 2026 revenue guidance to $6.42 billion and issued a preliminary fiscal 2027 outlook calling for at least 30% revenue growth.
Strong demand also shows in Ciena’s backlog, as the company ended Q3 with $8.5 billion on the books and projects to exit fiscal 2026 with over $10 billion. During the earnings call, executives stated, “The demand is absolutely there.” Supply remains the limit, and management doesn’t projects the market to return to balance before 2028.
Optical Links and AI Switches Ride One Spending Wave
Ciena sells optical networking equipment that links data centers, while Arista and Cisco Systems (NASDAQ:CSCO) sell the switches and routers inside them. Pluggable optics were a standout, with Ciena’s pluggables revenue more than doubling YoY in Q3 as the WaveLogic 6 Nano ramped. Notably, CSCO stock is practically unchanged at $107.06 today, so it’s not keeping pace with CIEN and ANET today.
Arista’s EtherLink switches power Ethernet-based AI fabrics in hyperscale data centers. Management frames the Arista 2.0 strategy around networking. The company sees networking as the “central nervous system” for infrastructure, and EtherLink adoption has spread to a broader roster of cloud, AI and neocloud customers.
Scale-across networks, which connect AI training clusters spread over multiple data centers, are Ciena’s next growth leg. Its RLS HyperRail line system, co-created with hyperscalers, is on track for initial customer adoption by year-end and material revenue through 2027. Co-packaged optics offer another lever, with revenue projects to begin in 2027 and grow into 2028 for Ciena.
Improving operating leverage is showing up in Ciena’s results too, with adjusted gross margin expanding 450 basis points YoY to 46.4%. The company’s chief executive asserted in the earnings release that “AI continues to drive compounding waves of network investment.”
Ciena’s growth carries concentration risk, since two customers made up 41.7% of its Q3 revenue. Its outlook also assumes continued AI infrastructure spending by cloud providers, stable optical component supply and no material change to tariff policy.
Next quarter’s results could show whether Ciena can hit its fiscal Q4 2026 revenue guidance of $1.75 billion under tight component supply. Traders will be tracking whether Ciena and Arista shares keep outpacing the iShares U.S. Technology ETF and the Invesco QQQ Trust.
Long-term supplier agreements running through 2029 could ease Ciena’s bottleneck, though recent moves in its shares show how quickly sentiment can turn. Investors may want to hold smaller share stakes until the supply squeeze resolves.

Cisco and NVIDIA Announce USFP: Expanding the Path to AI Connectivity
The Ultra-Dense Small Form-Factor Pluggable (USFP) is industry’s first pluggable form factor designed to help customers scale AI networks, providing a path to up to 12.8T of aggregate capacity while preserving proven deployment and serviceability models
As AI evolves from answering prompts to orchestrating complex, multi-step workflows, infrastructure demands are growing rapidly. From training and inference to emerging agentic AI systems, modern AI workloads depend on continuous communication across accelerators, applications, storage, and services, driving unprecedented requirements for bandwidth, responsiveness, and scale.
At Cisco, we believe the future of AI networking will be defined by how effectively silicon, systems, optics, software, and operations work together as a full-stack platform, enabling customers to scale AI with greater performance, efficiency, serviceability, and investment protection by optimizing every layer of the infrastructure together. Customers should not have to redesign their infrastructure or abandon established operational models to take advantage of the next generation of networking innovation.
Today, together with NVIDIA, we are announcing design plans for USFP, the industry’s first 400G-per-lane capable pluggable form factor designed to enable the next generation of AI Ethernet fabrics. USFP will provide a path supporting both 200G and 400G SerDes based systems and ASICs , helping customers scale from today’s 1.6T fabrics, with the ability to achieve 12.8T of overall pluggable capacity while preserving the benefits that have made pluggable optics successful.
As AI clusters grow across data centers, clouds, and edge environments, networks must carry significantly more traffic while balancing power, cooling, operational flexibility, and serviceability.
USFP is the next step in that journey. It addresses a critical industry challenge: delivering higher capacity AI fabrics without disrupting the manufacturing, deployment, and operational models that have enabled the scale and success of the pluggable ecosystem.
That perspective has shaped Cisco and NVIDIA’s collaboration for years. Together, we have helped customers build increasingly sophisticated infrastructure spanning networking, security, AI systems, and high-performance AI fabrics. Our work has been guided by a shared goal: helping customers accelerate AI adoption while maintaining flexibility, openness, and choice.
Preserving what works while advancing what’s next
The future of AI networking will not be defined by a single architectural approach. The industry continues to innovate across pluggable, near-packaged, co-packaged, and other emerging optical architectures, each with different advantages and tradeoffs. Customers will choose the technologies that best align with their operational requirements and long-term infrastructure strategies.
Organizations continue to value independently field replaceable modules, mature supply chains, interoperability across suppliers, and familiar serviceability models. These advantages become even more important as AI environments grow in scale and complexity.
USFP will extend those benefits into the next era of AI networking. It will provide a path toward higher capacity AI fabrics and higher density networking switch and compute equipment, while preserving the operational simplicity, openness, and ecosystem flexibility data center operators rely on today.
Accelerating the next generation of AI fabrics
USFP was designed with a simple objective: help AI networks scale efficiently.
With 16 lanes capable of operating at 400 Gb/s per lane, USFP will deliver 6.4T of aggregate capacity, four times the bandwidth density of today’s 1.6T pluggables. The architecture can scale to 32 lanes, providing a path to 12.8T of aggregate capacity. It also creates an opportunity for approximately 1.3x greater power efficiency through the use of 400G SerDes technology, helping operators manage growing power and cooling demands.
Together, these innovations create a foundation for higher-capacity AI Ethernet fabrics and continued innovation across the pluggable networking ecosystem.
To help customers scale AI infrastructure efficiently and sustainably, Cisco takes a full-stack, co-designed platform approach that combines silicon, high-density systems, optics, software, and operational expertise.
USFP reflects that philosophy. Rather than a standalone innovation, it is part of a broader platform vision that advances scale, efficiency, and performance while preserving the deployment, serviceability, and lifecycle models customers depend on.
USFP enables the industry to accelerate AI by building on the ecosystem models that have powered today’s AI networks. By combining a path to higher-capacity fabrics and improved efficiency with familiar operational practices, USFP helps customers scale AI infrastructure while maintaining the flexibility, interoperability, and consistency required at scale.
Cisco has long championed open ecosystems and industry collaboration to accelerate innovation and customer adoption. We see USFP as an extension of that approach, helping create a foundation for broad industry participation, interoperability, and long-term investment protection.
As AI networks continue to grow, Cisco and NVIDIA remain committed to delivering innovations that advance performance while preserving the operational foundations customers trust.

How Much Of Cisco Stock's Rise Did The Business Earn?
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 6:02 AM CDT 4 min read
Cisco Systems (CSCO) supplies businesses and the hyperscalers building AI infrastructure with networking and security products, along with services. The company's stock climbed 92% between late July 2021 and mid-October 2026, before dividends. A rally of that magnitude makes it natural to credit a growing business. So take a guess: how much of that rise came from Cisco selling more?
How Much Did Cisco's Sales Grow?
Cisco expanded its sales 27% over those five years. The company generated $63.3 billion in the twelve months to July 2026, compared with $49.8 billion in the twelve months to July 2021. That growth accounts for a little over a third of the stock's rise. Because the four changes multiply together, each portion of the rise is measured on a scale that lets them add up to 100%.
Expanding the business represents a real achievement. Yet nearly two thirds of the stock's advance came from somewhere else.
What Else Lifted Cisco Stock?
As the table details, most of the remaining gain came from what investors pay for Cisco's profit.
The price-to-earnings multiple, representing what investors pay for each dollar of profit, served as the largest source. Cisco's multiple rose from 22.1 to 32.0, and that expansion provided more than half of the stock's overall gain. The company also kept repurchasing stock, including during its latest quarter. The share count fell 5.8%, which added about a tenth of the rise. Meanwhile, Cisco's net margin, the share of sales the company keeps as profit, slipped slightly and pulled the price down a little.
So investors assigning a higher value to Cisco's profit did more for the stock than business growth did.
Can Margins And Multiples Keep Rising?
Multiples and margins cannot expand indefinitely, whereas sales can increase for as long as Cisco keeps selling more. The company's margin sat at 21.0% over the latest twelve months. That figure stands below the 26% it reached over the twelve months to the third quarter of fiscal 2019, marking its high for the past ten years.
By contrast, the multiple sits higher today than it did at 36 of the 40 quarter ends since fiscal 2017. The lift Cisco received from its multiple is therefore unlikely to repeat the way sales growth can.
What Cisco Would Need To Repeat Its Rise
If the margin, the multiple and the share count remained where they are, Cisco's sales would need to grow about 13.3% a year for the next five and a quarter years to give the stock the same rise. That future timeframe matches the window of the stock's historical rally. Over the past five years, Cisco grew sales 4.9% a year.
Sales are growing faster now. Sales rose 11.8% in fiscal 2026 and 17.6% in the quarter to July 2026. The Networking business led the expansion, growing 22.5% for the year. Management said about 6% of fiscal 2026 revenue came from AI infrastructure for hyperscalers, up from less than 2% in fiscal 2025.
Measured against the pace required for a repeat performance, Cisco's sales growth is the figure to watch in its next report, expected on or around November 10, 2026.

Prediction: Cisco Stock Could Surprise Wall Street by 2030
Cisco's CEO is calling it a networking super cycle, and the numbers behind that claim are hard to ignore. But reaching $200 by 2030 requires three specific things to go right, and at least one of them sits outside the…
Published October 17, 2026, 10:30am ET · 3 min read

Cisco Systems (NASDAQ:CSCO | CSCO Price Prediction | CSCO Price Prediction) sits in the middle of what its CEO calls a networking super cycle. Last quarter, product revenue rose 24% to $13.46B and networking climbed 28% to $9.79B. AI orders reached $9.30B for fiscal 2026.
Shares are up 43.91% YTD, yet they trade at $108.87 after a 4.2% drop today. Chuck Robbins said it directly: “We believe we’re only at the beginning of this super cycle.” So can Cisco reach $200 by 2030?
The stock has lost momentum. Shares fell 7.26% over the past week and 0.71% over the past month. They now trade below the 52-week high of $129.38. Investors are focused on margins.
Non-GAAP gross margin slipped to 66.3% from 68.4% as lower-margin AI hardware took a bigger share of sales. Management also highlighted memory costs and uneven hyperscaler order timing. With a beta of 0.979, Cisco usually tracks the broader market, which makes a sharp one-day drop a clear sign of investor nerves.
Wall Street Sees 25.1% Upside. Our Model Says 19.5%
The consensus target is $136.16, an upside of 25.1%. It rests on 5 Strong Buy, 14 Buy, 10 Hold and 0 Sell ratings. Our one-year base case is $130.14, a 19.5% gain. The scenarios run from $109.27 in the bear case to $138.12 in the bull case, and model confidence is high at 0.9.
In my view, both expectations underestimate Cisco’s earnings. Earnings grew 52.1% year over year, yet only 66% of analysts rate the stock bullish. Ten Holds on a company guiding to $5.05 to $5.11 in fiscal 2027 non-GAAP EPS strike me as too conservative.
Here’s What It Takes for Cisco to Reach $200
To get to $200 from today’s price of $108.87 would require a gain of 83.7%.
With forward EPS of $5.146, a price of $200 implies a forward P/E of 39x. Our base case of $130.14 already implies 26x, so the bold target requires 13x of additional multiple expansion.
Today’s valuation looks steep, but the math shifts over time. If EPS compounds at the 9.23% consensus growth rate through fiscal 2030, it reaches about $6.71, and $200 works out to roughly 30x.
Earnings growth does most of the lifting. An adjustment factor of 1.125 reflects technology sector momentum and strong earnings acceleration, with the five-year bull case already reaching $187.86.
The catalysts keep coming. Cisco expects AI infrastructure revenue of $7.5B in fiscal 2027, roughly double fiscal 2026. Recent releases highlighted Splunk advancements for trusted AI, new agentic collaboration experiences and scalability and openness at OCP 2026.
Robbins added: “The network remains an absolute critical factor as to whether AI deployments succeed or fail.” Cisco is one of several picks-and-shovels names gaining from the data-center expansion (we rounded up seven of these AI infrastructure suppliers, networking included, in a free report here).
A major risk is that hyperscaler AI spending cools before enterprise demand can fill the gap.
Where Cisco Trades Today vs Its Earnings Power
At $108.87, Cisco trades at 21x forward EPS. That’s a reasonable multiple for a company guiding to $72.2B to $73.4B in fiscal 2027 revenue, up from $63.33B in fiscal 2026.
Shares sit between a 52-week low of $67.32 and a high of $129.38. Over 10 years, the stock has returned 383.19%. A 21x multiple on accelerating earnings leaves room for the bull case to play out.
$200 Is a Stretch, But Here’s Why It’s Possible
Hitting $200 by 2030 would take an 83.7% gain. I see it as a stretch, though a reachable one. Three things need to go right. AI infrastructure revenue has to keep growing past $7.5B. Security growth needs to improve to high single digits, as management expects. Operating margins also have to hold near 35% while gross margin slips.
A sharp pullback in hyperscaler capex would undermine the thesis. Returns at this level shouldn’t be expected every year, but we’ve outlined the path for how Cisco could reach $200 in 2030.

Cisco vs. IBM: Why the Stock Nobody Wants Could Be the Better Retirement Buy
One tech giant is up over 50% this year while the other has fallen out of favor with Wall Street, and for retirees living off dividend income, that divergence points toward a clear winner that most investors are overlooking.
Published October 13, 2026, 11:45am ET · 3 min read
Abstract financial data graph featuring candlestick and line charts © Abstract financial data graph featuring candlestick and line charts (Shutterstock.com) by hateeyes
Cisco Systems (NASDAQ:CSCO | CSCO Price Prediction) or IBM (NYSE:IBM): which tech dividend stock makes the stronger case for a retirement-focused investor right now? Cisco is the momentum story. It is up 52.27% year to date on an AI networking boom. IBM is the yield story, down 19.88% year to date after a second-quarter earnings miss. For income, the stock that has fallen out of favor has the stronger case.
IBM’s quarterly dividend of $1.69 works out to a 2.91% yield at the current $232.58 share price. Cisco’s $0.42 quarterly payout yields just 1.46% at $115.19. Cisco’s own rally caused the gap. The stock is up 72.64% over the past year, which contracted its yield. Put the same dollars into IBM and you collect about twice the income. Winner: IBM.
Dividend Safety: IBM’s Cash Cushion Runs Deeper
IBM generated $14.73 billion in free cash flow in 2025, up 25.29%, and paid $6.255 billion in dividends. That means the dividend used only 42% of free cash flow. Even in the quarter that missed estimates, free cash flow rose 70.36% to $2.54 billion.
Cisco’s fiscal 2026 operating cash flow of $14.177 billion, minus $1.41 billion in capital spending, left about $12.77 billion. Dividends of $6.553 billion took 51% of that. Add buybacks and total capital returns reached 99% of free cash flow. Buybacks give Cisco room to adjust, but the dividend has a thinner buffer.
Cisco does win on earnings coverage. Its dividend is 39% of fiscal 2026 non-GAAP EPS of $4.33, compared with 60% of IBM’s trailing EPS of $11.25. IBM also carries $61.3 billion in debt and faces a securities fraud inquiry. Still, companies pay dividends with cash, and IBM has more cash to spare. Winner: IBM.
Dividend Growth: Cisco Raises Much Faster
IBM just raised its dividend for the 31st consecutive year, and its dividend record going back to 1999 shows a higher payout every year. The raises are small, though. The quarterly payout went from $1.64 in 2021 to $1.69 today, a gain of just 3%. Cisco, on its 15th consecutive annual increase, went from $0.37 to $0.42 over the same stretch, up 13.5%.
Cisco’s business supports faster raises. Fiscal 2027 EPS guidance is $5.05 to $5.11, and the company expects AI infrastructure revenue to about double to $7.5 billion. IBM’s mainframe revenue fell 42% in the second quarter and operating income dropped 19.67%. Its chief executive now expects “constant currency revenue growth in the range of four-to-five percent”. Winner: Cisco.
Verdict: IBM Is the Retiree’s Income Stock
IBM comes out on top in two of three categories, and both wins matter most to someone living off dividends. A 2.91% yield supported by a 42% free cash flow payout puts more cash in a retiree’s pocket every quarter. A beta of 0.724 means less volatility. The selloff also brought down the price. IBM trades at a forward P/E of 17, while Cisco sits near 27 times fiscal 2026 non-GAAP earnings. Barron’s wrote that IBM stock looks cheap, but Wall Street isn’t buying it yet.
Cisco makes the stronger case for investors a decade or more from retirement. They can accept a thin yield today in exchange for faster dividend growth and AI-driven gains in the share price. For a retiree who needs income now, IBM is the stronger stock, and the broader goal of living off the checks without selling shares is the whole basis of a free dividend ladder guide we put together here. Watch IBM’s next quarterly report for signs of a mainframe recovery and news on the fraud inquiry. For Cisco, the test is whether fiscal first-quarter revenue lands within its $18.0 billion to $18.2 billion guidance.

Wed, October 14, 2026 at 9:07 AM CDT 5 min read
Cisco Systems, Inc. (NASDAQ:CSCO) has an opportunity to turn artificial-intelligence infrastructure spending and network upgrades into stronger cash generation. Fiscal-2026 net income increased 30% to $13.3 billion, but operating cash flow stayed near $14.2 billion. Reported earnings also benefited from higher unrealized investment gains, which increased profit without generating operating cash. Cisco's cybersecurity business adds another growth avenue as companies strengthen their defenses against evolving threats. Find our rankings of cybersecurity stocks here.
Cisco Systems, Inc. (NASDAQ:CSCO) trades at approximately 20x forward earnings and 32x trailing earnings. The earnings outlook combines operating growth with accounting exclusions. Fiscal-2027 guidance calls for GAAP EPS of $4.00–$4.06, against $3.33 in fiscal 2026, and company-defined non-GAAP adjusted EPS of $5.05–$5.11. Adjustments include stock compensation, acquisition-related amortization, and restructuring. The lower forward multiple should not be read as pure profit growth.
Arista Networks, Inc. (NYSE:ANET) is the closest operating comparison because it competes in network switching. Its 45.4% second-quarter GAAP operating margin sets a high profitability benchmark for Cisco Systems, Inc. (NASDAQ:CSCO). Hewlett Packard Enterprise Company (NYSE:HPE) has greater server exposure, and its inventory commitments create a different cash-conversion test. The 20x forward valuation looks reasonable only if its fourth-quarter cash rebound persists.
Installed Networks Support Growth, but Require Funding
Cisco Systems, Inc. (NASDAQ:CSCO) benefits from established enterprise networks, customer relationships, and the cost of replacing integrated equipment and software. Management says more than half its customers purchase both campus and data-center networking. That breadth creates opportunities to sell upgrades into existing relationships and spread development and support expenses across more revenue. Billionaire Ken Fisher also holds a position in Cisco, reflecting investor interest in the networking company. See which other AI stocks are on the billionaire's radar.
AI demand strengthens that opportunity. Cisco Systems, Inc. (NASDAQ:CSCO) booked $9.3 billion in hyperscaler AI infrastructure orders in fiscal 2026 and recognized about $4 billion in associated revenue. Management expects $7.5 billion of AI infrastructure revenue in fiscal 2027. The difference between bookings and sales matters because large AI orders can arrive well before shareholder cash.
Revenue guidance of $72.2 billion–$73.4 billion implies approximately 15% growth at the midpoint. The adjusted EPS midpoint implies about 17% growth from fiscal-2026 adjusted EPS of $4.33. Those forecasts require operating leverage as shipments increase, while memory shortages and higher component prices can absorb part of the benefit.
Subscription revenue gives Cisco Systems, Inc. (NASDAQ:CSCO) a recurring base, but it increased only about 1% to $32.0 billion in fiscal 2026. Maintaining that base supports investment; it does not yet establish accelerating software cash growth. Hardware expansion still requires inventory purchases before customer payments arrive, and competitive pricing can limit the profit retained from additional shipments.
A Better Quarter Has Not Removed the Cash Burden
Cisco Systems, Inc. (NASDAQ:CSCO) generated $5.4 billion of fourth-quarter operating cash flow, up 27%. That is meaningful evidence against treating the annual cash plateau as permanent. Fiscal 2026 also included the final $2.3 billion U.S. transition-tax payment, removing one specific future cash obligation.
Working capital nevertheless remains demanding. Annual inventory and financing-receivable movements absorbed approximately $2.5 billion and $1.8 billion, respectively. Both continued consuming cash in the fourth quarter, when their combined use approached $2.8 billion. Higher deferred revenue and other liabilities helped offset those demands. The rebound did not come from releasing inventory or collecting down customer financing.
Offering payment flexibility can support equipment sales, but customer financing earns its keep only when collections justify the risk. Persistently larger financing balances would tie up capital and reduce the cash available for distributions, even if reported sales and earnings continued growing.
Non-GAAP free cash flow, defined as operating cash flow less purchases of property and equipment, declined 4% to $12.8 billion as capital spending increased. Dividends and buybacks consumed approximately 99% of that amount. Sustaining distributions alongside growth investment therefore depends on better conversion, not simply higher accounting profit.
Cisco Systems, Inc. (NASDAQ:CSCO) produced $13.3 billion of free cash flow in fiscal 2025 before the latest decline. The business has demonstrated substantial cash generation, but stronger AI demand now brings heavier funding requirements. At 20x forward earnings, shareholders need growth that increases cash after those commitments. More sales alone would provide little valuation protection if funding needs absorbed the additional profit.
Cisco Systems, Inc. (NASDAQ:CSCO) looks reasonably valued at 20x forward earnings if the fourth-quarter cash recovery becomes sustained growth. Installed relationships and stronger infrastructure demand make that outcome credible. It requires earnings growth to produce more cash after investment, with inventory and financing needs growing more slowly than sales. Continued working-capital expansion alongside flat free cash flow would make the valuation demanding, even if orders remained strong.

Management expects fiscal 2027 GAAP EPS of $4.00–$4.06, versus $3.33 in fiscal 2026. Lower expected taxes also support growth: guidance assumes a 14.5% GAAP tax rate, versus 17.1% in fiscal 2026. Meanwhile, $1.39 billion of pretax net investment gains lifted fiscal 2026 reported earnings. Company-defined non-GAAP profits exclude stock compensation, acquired-intangible amortization and restructuring. Sustainable earnings require operating gains beyond tax benefits and investment returns.

Cisco Systems, Inc. (NASDAQ:CSCO) carries a 20x forward P/E, compared with 17x in 2025. Stronger AI networking demand and higher earnings expectations support the increase. Maintaining that premium requires profitable software revenue after the equipment upgrade wave fades.
Cisco Systems, Inc. (NASDAQ:CSCO) reported companywide annualized recurring revenue, or ARR, of $32.1 billion, up 3%, while fiscal fourth-quarter networking revenue rose 28%. ARR measures the annualized revenue run rate of active contracts, including subscriptions and maintenance. It does not isolate networking renewals from initial sales. Retention and customer expansion show how existing accounts contribute to growth.
Management says AI-assisted support is improving renewal rates. Lower service costs would make renewals more profitable, provided discounts and cheaper tiers do not erode those savings.

Hardware expansion absorbs working capital. Renewals could improve cash generation without comparable inventory investment. Investors should track renewal pricing, downgrades, and service margins, consistent with testing subscription growth against underlying profitability.
Higher memory costs and a heavier hardware mix reduced quarterly adjusted product gross margin by 2.7 percentage points. Software can offset that pressure when incremental revenue exceeds hosting, development and support costs. Discounted renewals could preserve customer numbers while weakening earnings, limiting how much of the business deserves a premium for recurring earnings.
Cisco Systems, Inc. (NASDAQ:CSCO) can justify 20x forward earnings if renewals preserve pricing and improve cash generation as hardware growth slows. Cisco stock shed nearly 5% on Tuesday after Piper Sandler analyst James Fish cut the firm's price target on the networking equipment company to $125 from $132, while holding a Neutral rating in place.
Fish and his team pointed to reduced price-to-earnings multiple assumptions, with the analysts expressing concern that the industry's growth trajectory may be approaching its ceiling, according to CNBC. Cisco stock closed Tuesday at $106.44.
On Wall Street, Cisco holds a consensus Buy rating, and analysts' average price target stands at $133.86, according to Benzinga. Also on the analyst front, Deutsche Bank started coverage with a Buy rating and a $135 price target on September 1, while HSBC moved to a Hold rating with a $120 target on August 14, Benzinga reported.
Shares reached an all-time peak in June and have gained 57% over the past year, buoyed by revenue growth tied to surging artificial intelligence investment.
The Piper Sandler move comes roughly a month after Cisco reported fourth-quarter revenue of $17.25 billion, beating analyst expectations and posting record annual results, though Cisco stock fell in after-hours trading following that announcement. Skeptical analysts countered that underlying sales expansion would retreat to single-digit territory. Piper Sandler described the company's own outlook as "conservative" relative to what broader market demand would support, according to CNBC.
Cisco CEO Chuck Robbins addressed the cautious tone on guidance last month. "We're starting a new fiscal year. We're operating in incredible markets," Robbins told CNBC's Jim Cramer. "But it's also a time that we're going to start the year being a little bit prudent."

Networking hardware is leading a broad technology rebound, and suppliers of optical links and Ethernet switches for AI data centers are drawing the biggest buying. By Monday afternoon, Ciena Corporation (NYSE:CIEN | CIEN Price Prediction) stock was up 4% to $347.48. Meanwhile, Arista Networks (NYSE:ANET) stock also climbed 4%, hitting $183.32 and keeping pace with the gain in Ciena shares.

A sharp pullback in Ciena and Arista shares over the prior week came before the bounce. Hyperscaler spending on AI infrastructure remains the core support for Ciena and Arista. Both companies build the networks that move data between and inside AI data centers.
Supply Limits Keep Ciena’s Backlog Growing
Ciena’s fiscal Q3 2026 results showed adjusted EPS of $2.11 against a $1.73 consensus. The company’s revenue rose 37% year over year (YoY) to $1.67 billion.
Cloud providers did the biggest spending for Ciena, accounting for 53% of revenue on 82% YoY growth. Management raised its fiscal 2026 revenue guidance to $6.42 billion and issued a preliminary fiscal 2027 outlook calling for at least 30% revenue growth.
Strong demand also shows in Ciena’s backlog, as the company ended Q3 with $8.5 billion on the books and projects to exit fiscal 2026 with over $10 billion. During the earnings call, executives stated, “The demand is absolutely there.” Supply remains the limit, and management doesn’t projects the market to return to balance before 2028.
Optical Links and AI Switches Ride One Spending Wave
Ciena sells optical networking equipment that links data centers, while Arista and Cisco Systems (NASDAQ:CSCO) sell the switches and routers inside them. Pluggable optics were a standout, with Ciena’s pluggables revenue more than doubling YoY in Q3 as the WaveLogic 6 Nano ramped. Notably, CSCO stock is practically unchanged at $107.06 today, so it’s not keeping pace with CIEN and ANET today.
Arista’s EtherLink switches power Ethernet-based AI fabrics in hyperscale data centers. Management frames the Arista 2.0 strategy around networking. The company sees networking as the “central nervous system” for infrastructure, and EtherLink adoption has spread to a broader roster of cloud, AI and neocloud customers.
Scale-across networks, which connect AI training clusters spread over multiple data centers, are Ciena’s next growth leg. Its RLS HyperRail line system, co-created with hyperscalers, is on track for initial customer adoption by year-end and material revenue through 2027. Co-packaged optics offer another lever, with revenue projects to begin in 2027 and grow into 2028 for Ciena.
Improving operating leverage is showing up in Ciena’s results too, with adjusted gross margin expanding 450 basis points YoY to 46.4%. The company’s chief executive asserted in the earnings release that “AI continues to drive compounding waves of network investment.”
Ciena’s growth carries concentration risk, since two customers made up 41.7% of its Q3 revenue. Its outlook also assumes continued AI infrastructure spending by cloud providers, stable optical component supply and no material change to tariff policy.
Next quarter’s results could show whether Ciena can hit its fiscal Q4 2026 revenue guidance of $1.75 billion under tight component supply. Traders will be tracking whether Ciena and Arista shares keep outpacing the iShares U.S. Technology ETF and the Invesco QQQ Trust.
Long-term supplier agreements running through 2029 could ease Ciena’s bottleneck, though recent moves in its shares show how quickly sentiment can turn. Investors may want to hold smaller share stakes until the supply squeeze resolves.

The Ultra-Dense Small Form-Factor Pluggable (USFP) is industry’s first pluggable form factor designed to help customers scale AI networks, providing a path to up to 12.8T of aggregate capacity while preserving proven deployment and serviceability models
As AI evolves from answering prompts to orchestrating complex, multi-step workflows, infrastructure demands are growing rapidly. From training and inference to emerging agentic AI systems, modern AI workloads depend on continuous communication across accelerators, applications, storage, and services, driving unprecedented requirements for bandwidth, responsiveness, and scale.
At Cisco, we believe the future of AI networking will be defined by how effectively silicon, systems, optics, software, and operations work together as a full-stack platform, enabling customers to scale AI with greater performance, efficiency, serviceability, and investment protection by optimizing every layer of the infrastructure together. Customers should not have to redesign their infrastructure or abandon established operational models to take advantage of the next generation of networking innovation.
Today, together with NVIDIA, we are announcing design plans for USFP, the industry’s first 400G-per-lane capable pluggable form factor designed to enable the next generation of AI Ethernet fabrics. As AI clusters grow across data centers, clouds, and edge environments, networks must carry significantly more traffic while balancing power, cooling, operational flexibility, and serviceability.
USFP is the next step in that journey. It addresses a critical industry challenge: delivering higher capacity AI fabrics without disrupting the manufacturing, deployment, and operational models that have enabled the scale and success of the pluggable ecosystem.
That perspective has shaped Cisco and NVIDIA’s collaboration for years. Together, we have helped customers build increasingly sophisticated infrastructure spanning networking, security, AI systems, and high-performance AI fabrics. Our work has been guided by a shared goal: helping customers accelerate AI adoption while maintaining flexibility, openness, and choice.
Preserving what works while advancing what’s next
The future of AI networking will not be defined by a single architectural approach. The industry continues to innovate across pluggable, near-packaged, co-packaged, and other emerging optical architectures, each with different advantages and tradeoffs. Customers will choose the technologies that best align with their operational requirements and long-term infrastructure strategies.
Organizations continue to value independently field replaceable modules, mature supply chains, interoperability across suppliers, and familiar serviceability models. These advantages become even more important as AI environments grow in scale and complexity.
USFP will extend those benefits into the next era of AI networking. It will provide a path toward higher capacity AI fabrics and higher density networking switch and compute equipment, while preserving the operational simplicity, openness, and ecosystem flexibility data center operators rely on today.
Accelerating the next generation of AI fabrics
USFP was designed with a simple objective: help AI networks scale efficiently.
With 16 lanes capable of operating at 400 Gb/s per lane, USFP will deliver 6.4T of aggregate capacity, four times the bandwidth density of today’s 1.6T pluggables. The architecture can scale to 32 lanes, providing a path to 12.8T of aggregate capacity. It also creates an opportunity for approximately 1.3x greater power efficiency through the use of 400G SerDes technology, helping operators manage growing power and cooling demands.
Together, these innovations create a foundation for higher-capacity AI Ethernet fabrics and continued innovation across the pluggable networking ecosystem.
To help customers scale AI infrastructure efficiently and sustainably, Cisco takes a full-stack, co-designed platform approach that combines silicon, high-density systems, optics, software, and operational expertise.

How Much Of Cisco Stock's Rise Did The Business Earn?
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 6:02 AM CDT 4 min read
Cisco Systems (CSCO) supplies businesses and the hyperscalers building AI infrastructure with networking and security products, along with services. The company's stock climbed 92% between late July 2021 and mid-October 2026, before dividends. A rally of that magnitude makes it natural to credit a growing business. So take a guess: how much of that rise came from Cisco selling more?
How Much Did Cisco's Sales Grow?
Cisco expanded its sales 27% over those five years. The company generated $63.3 billion in the twelve months to July 2026, compared with $49.8 billion in the twelve months to July 2021. That growth accounts for a little over a third of the stock's rise. Because the four changes multiply together, each portion of the rise is measured on a scale that lets them add up to 100%.
Expanding the business represents a real achievement. Yet nearly two thirds of the stock's advance came from somewhere else.
What Else Lifted Cisco Stock?
As the table details, most of the remaining gain came from what investors pay for Cisco's profit.
The price-to-earnings multiple, representing what investors pay for each dollar of profit, served as the largest source. Cisco's multiple rose from 22.1 to 32.0, and that expansion provided more than half of the stock's overall gain. The company also kept repurchasing stock, including during its latest quarter. The share count fell 5.8%, which added about a tenth of the rise. Meanwhile, Cisco's net margin, the share of sales the company keeps as profit, slipped slightly and pulled the price down a little.
So investors assigning a higher value to Cisco's profit did more for the stock than business growth did.
Can Margins And Multiples Keep Rising?
Multiples and margins cannot expand indefinitely, whereas sales can increase for as long as Cisco keeps selling more. The company's margin sat at 21.0% over the latest twelve months. That figure stands below the 26% it reached over the twelve months to the third quarter of fiscal 2019, marking its high for the past ten years.
By contrast, the multiple sits higher today than it did at 36 of the 40 quarter ends since fiscal 2017. The lift Cisco received from its multiple is therefore unlikely to repeat the way sales growth can.
What Cisco Would Need To Repeat Its Rise
If the margin, the multiple and the share count remained where they are, Cisco's sales would need to grow about 13.3% a year for the next five and a quarter years to give the stock the same rise. That future timeframe matches the window of the stock's historical rally. Over the past five years, Cisco grew sales 4.9% a year.
Sales are growing faster now. Sales rose 11.8% in fiscal 2026 and 17.6% in the quarter to July 2026. The Networking business led the expansion, growing 22.5% for the year. Management said about 6% of fiscal 2026 revenue came from AI infrastructure for hyperscalers, up from less than 2% in fiscal 2025.
Measured against the pace required for a repeat performance, Cisco's sales growth is the figure to watch in its next report, expected on or around November 10, 2026.
